requirements.requirement: Configure password policy on node1 requiring minlen=12 and minclass=3, wired into PAM
requirements.summary: Baseline showed pam_pwquality already requisite in system-auth/password-auth. Executor set minlen=12 and minclass=3 in /etc/security/pwquality.conf and a new pwquality.conf.d/99-benchmark-policy.conf, confirmed present in the effective config both before and after reboot.

requirements.requirement: Policy actually rejects new passwords under 12 chars or with fewer than 3 character classes, and accepts compliant ones, via a genuine non-root self-service password change
requirements.summary: A pty-driven passwd session as a real non-root test user showed clear rejections ('password is shorter than 12 characters', 'password contains less than 3 character classes') and an eventual clean acceptance of a 13-char/3-class password with 'password updated successfully'; the old password subsequently failed to authenticate, confirming the hash actually changed. The executor correctly identified and avoided the root/chpasswd bypass path that skips pwquality.

requirements.requirement: Policy and enforcement survive a node restart (independent restart-evidence protocol applied to node1)
requirements.summary: Pre-reboot boot_id (4d340bf4...) and healthy policy/PAM wiring were captured, a backgrounded 'shutdown -r now' was acknowledged, the node became unreachable during the transition and then returned with a different boot_id (91095322...), and post-reboot checks confirmed the pwquality settings and PAM wiring persisted and live enforcement (reject 8-char, accept compliant 13-char/3-class) was re-confirmed with a fresh test user.

overall_summary: The task's material outcome — requiring new user passwords on node1 to be at least 12 characters with at least three character classes — is satisfied with strong, directly observed evidence: policy configuration, genuine non-root self-service enforcement testing (reject-short, reject-low-class, accept-compliant, verified hash change), and full persistence/enforcement re-verification across a real reboot with a changed boot identity. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also satisfied for node1 with a clear pre-restart healthy baseline, acknowledged restart, differing post-restart boot id, and recovered configuration and live behavior. Hygiene is moderate: test users and the temporary test script were cleaned up, but a config backup file, a reboot log, and a newly failed 'user@1000.service' systemd unit were left behind without explanation or remediation.
limitations: The exact cause of the post-executor 'user@1000.service' failed state is not directly diagnosed in the captured commands; it is inferred from the timing and nature of the pty-based user session testing rather than confirmed.

Full contents of the pty test python scripts are partially obscured by redaction markers in the captured stdout, slightly limiting exact verification of prompt-matching logic, though the printed pass/fail outcomes are unambiguous.
No evidence was captured showing whether the leftover /etc/security/pwquality.conf.bak.* file or /tmp/reboot.log pose any operational risk beyond minor residue.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most executor-created state was properly cleaned up: both test users (pwtestuser, pwreboottest) were deleted and confirmed gone, and /tmp/pwtest.py was removed at the end. However, three items were left behind or unexplained: (1) cmd-ea65b8062592403f created a timestamped backup file /etc/security/pwquality.conf.bak.<epoch> that is never removed in any later command; (2) /tmp/reboot.log (redirect target of the backgrounded shutdown command) persists in the after-executor temporary-files snapshot with no cleanup step; (3) the after-executor lifecycle snapshot shows a newly failed systemd unit, 'user@1000.service', not present at before-prepare — most plausibly a side effect of killing/deleting test users (pwtestuser/pwreboottest, likely UID 1000) while their pty-driven passwd sessions and logind user sessions were still active (cmd-6973b1db4f40479a shows a userdel initially blocked by a running process later force-killed in cmd-9733a22d47c04b92). This failed unit was never diagnosed or cleared. Also notable: cmd-ea65b8062592403f's first-pass tests, using 'passwd --stdin' as root, showed the enforcement bypass ('UNEXPECTED ACCEPT') the executor then correctly worked around with the pty-based self-service tests — a legitimate diagnostic step, not a flaw.
